newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian economy to grow 2.0 pct in 1997 -employers.
newsitem.headline: Belgian economy to grow 2.0 pct in 1997 -employers.

text.p: The Belgian economy will grow at a real, inflation-adjusted rate of two percent this year, running on the joint motors of exports and investments, the Belgian employers' federation (FEB) said on Tuesday.
The forecast is in line with the FEB's earlier predictions and is despite the drag caused by the dire state of consumer confidence, economics director Baudouin Velge told a news conference.
It is also in line with the latest estimates from the Belgian central bank.
"In general one notes a broad economic uplift in the European Union, which translates into a good export performance in the first quarter of 1997," the FEB said.
"Furthermore, the results of a recent survey on investments confirm the view that they will rise strongly this year despite the disappointing rise in the first quarter," it added.
"These two factors will support growth because the news from the consumer side is hardly positive.
"Taking account of these elements the FEB maintains its view that real economic growth will be 2.0 percent this year," it concluded.
Growth was 2.3 percent in the first quarter of this year compared with the first three months of 1996. It was the best figure since mid-1995.
Belgian corporate investments are expected to rise by seven percent this year. Investment in construction of homes is expected to rise strongly due to a special cut in value added tax for the sector.

The strong dollar and pound have helped lift Belgian exports. Velge expected this to remain the case for the rest of the year, helping to offset the effect of disappointing economic figures for the Netherlands and France.

Noting that the advent of the EU's single currency would help European exporters, Velge said one of the determining factors in future growth in Belgium and elsewhere would be the evolution of salary costs, which he said were far too high.

He rejected outright a growing move to cut the basic working week to 32 hours across the board on the basis that jobs were becoming far more specialised and there were often not enough adequately trained and qualified people to fill vacancies created either by short working or holidays.
